lectures.title: Three Trees: Widget Tree, Element Tree & Render Tree

cues.en: So let's get started.
And before we have that look at keys,
let's have a look at trees first.
Because when working with Flutter,
you are essentially working with three trees,
though two of those three trees are typically invisible
to you as a developer.
You do, of course, know the widget tree,
which you're building.
When building a Flutter app,
you're dealing with widgets,
and it's this combination of widgets,
this nesting of widgets into each other,
which we typically call a widget tree.
But Flutter also knows a so-called element tree
and a render tree,
and it helps to understand what these trees are all about
and how they are related.
Now, as mentioned,
the widget tree is simply this combination of widgets
in your code.
So if a Flutter developer takes a look at some Flutter code
and sees all these widgets combined with each other
and nested into each other,
they would typically call that combination
the so-called Widget Tree.
But Flutter actually takes that widget tree
and translates it into the element tree,
which is simply in memory representation of your widgets.
Now, with that, I don't mean the widget objects
that are created by instantiating the widget classes.
So your classes that extend state full
or state less widgets,
but I mean additional objects
which are connected to the widget objects though,
which are created in memory by Flutter.
And Flutter creates these extra element objects in memory
to be able to efficiently determine required UI updates.
Now these element objects as mentioned,
are related to your widget objects.
For example, when a widget is first encountered
and its build method is called for the first time,
Flutter will thereafter create a fitting element object
and store that in memory.
But the build method is typically called quite frequently,
for example, because you called set state
in a stateful widget.
In that case, that widgets build method
would be called again,
and all child widgets build methods would be called again,
because Flutter needs to check that entire part
of the widget tree
to make sure that the state update is represented correctly.
But Flutter does not necessarily recreate
all those element objects.
Instead, it only creates new elements
if you added new widgets,
or it removes elements from the elementary
if widgets were removed,
for example, because of some conditional code.
So elements are actually reused if possible.
They are not recreated all the time.
They are created initially
when a widgets build method is called for the first time,
but for subsequent cause of a widget's build method,
elements are instead reused.
But it's this element tree that's then used
to determine which UI should actually be rendered
on the screen.
And that's where the render tree comes into play,
because the render tree is the combination
of visible UI building blocks,
so the things you can see on the screen.
And creating that render tree
and updating the UI and the render tree, therefore,
actually takes quite a lot of work.
It has quite a big performance impact,
and therefore, Flutter is built such that it really tries
to avoid touching that render tree,
and it only re-renders parts of the UI
when UI updates are needed.
And if an update is needed,
is determined with help of that element tree.
Because in the end,
you can think of this UI updating process like this.
When the build method is called,
Flutter checks the element tree
and reuses existing elements as needed,
and then thereafter, it compares the new element tree
to the old element tree.
And if there are any differences,
those differences are applied to the render tree
and the UI is updated.
But of course, Flutter will not re-render the entire screen
just because one tiny part of it needs to be updated.
Instead, it really takes care
to only partially update the UI
and re-render the parts that need updating.
Now, as a developer,
you don't need to worry about the element and render tree,
Flutter manages those trees for you.
You build your widgets with their build methods,
and that's it.

you should always also understand
what's happening behind the scenes,
